speakeroldname: Hon. Robert H. Winters (Minister of Resources and Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 8 the hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser) asked me if I intended to table the report being prepared by Messrs. J. D. Woods and Gordon on the organization and business practices of the national film board. At that time I had not received the report, and while I did not give a definite answer, I indicated that I expected to table it.
The investigation was undertaken at my request after consultation with Right Hon. Vincent Massey, chairman of the royal commission on the arts, letters and sciences. The terms of reference under which the investigation was conducted were discussed with Mr. Massey, who informed me that they would serve his purpose as well and that the resulting report would be useful to him.
The report has now been received, and I have given preliminary consideration to its recommendations, some of which are along lines on which the government and the board have already been proceeding, others of which will require special consideration by the film commissioner, the board and the government.
Meanwhile, I feel that it would be of advantage to make the report public so that hon. members and others interested may also have the opportunity of considering its recommendations and the reasons given for them. I would accordingly ask the leave
of the house to table a copy of the report. In offering to table it, I should emphasize that it is not a governmental document which there is any obligation to table, and that I should not like my action in this case to be construed in the future as a precedent which would prevent the government from securing confidential expert advice in dealing with administrative problems.
In the present case I think there is something to be gained by discussion of the problems set forth in the report and of the solutions suggested.
I am gratified, and I am sure most hon. members will be equally gratified, by the tribute paid by these experienced business consultants to the achievements of the board and to the high level of service of the board's employees.
The report indicates that where there are weaknesses in the organization and methods of the board, they are in most cases the natural outcome of a rapid period of growth under the exceptional circumstances of war. The situation was aggravated by the obviously inefficient arrangements for housing the board's activities, which were, in turn, the inevitable result of the space problem all government agencies have faced during and since the war.
I shall not attempt today to indicate how far and how rapidly the government will be able to implement the recommendations, some of which incidentally do not call for immediate action. Since I asked Messrs. J. D. Woods and Gordon to make the investigation, Mr. W. Arthur Irwin has been appointed government film commissioner, and, as the report itself suggests, the commissioner should have ample opportunity to review the organization and activities of the board before final decisions are made.
I should like to take advantage of this occasion to say a word about another matter relating to the film board. The screening of the national film board, undertaken last year in conformity with the government's established security regulations, has proceeded to the point where it was possible for me on February 21 to direct the commissioner to inform all government departments and agencies concerned that the board was in a position to undertake work of a secret nature. This of course applies to the Department of

National Film Board
National Defence, and on the same day I advised the Minister of National Defence accordingly.
The screening of all employees of the board has been completed. Action has been taken in the case of a very few employees about whose trustworthiness the board was unable to feel any definite assurance. I hope no hon. member will press for details in the house about these matters, at least not until he has discussed confidentially with me any case that may be giving him concern. The reason is the one I gave the house on December 7, and which I should now like to repeat, namely that:
It would be a grave injustice to such persons- against whom there is no charge of wrongdoing, but merely the absence of satisfactory evidence of trustworthiness-to proclaim their names publicly and thereby injure their reputations and their chances of alternative employment. What I wish to emphasize is that it is not the government which would be hurt by publicity but the men and women whose reliability and trustworthiness are under examination; and nobody wants to be unfair and unjust to individuals.
I think I should make one other point. The process of screening of government employees is a continuous one. There is the usual turnover, with new employees being taken on; but it is the earnest hope of all who have been concerned with this matter that the number of cases of untrustworthiness in the future will be as rare as they have so far proved to be.

I should like to thank the minister for tabling the report. I think it is in the interests of the welfare of the national film board for the present and the future. I hope there is more than one copy of it; otherwise members will not have a chance to go through it.
I do not want any of the details that the minister suggests should not be asked for, but would the minister care to indicate the number of the cases to which he has referred?
No.

More than there are on your side.

I should like to ask a supplementary question, as to how the screening

was carried on in connection with the three employees of the film board to whom reference -has been made. Were they given a hearing before their employment was terminated? What opportunity did they have to meet the charges, if we can call them charges, that were made against them? Was any such opportunity afforded?

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert McCubbin (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PRODUCTION IN 1949 AND EFFECT ON BUTTER CONSUMPTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a short statement. Last night, in the course of discussion of Bill No. 17 in committee, the. hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) asked some questions as to the manufacture of oleomargarine in Canada. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) answered and said that the manufacture of oleomargarine in Canada was better than 3 million pounds per month, making an approximate total of 40 million pounds for the year 1949. Some exception was taken to this statement, and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) asked that the matter be laid over, and requested that I make a statement today.
The total amount of oleomargarine manufactured in Canada last year was 73,958,000 pounds, and owing to the manufacture of oleomargarine the consumption of butter decreased in 1949 compared with 1948 to the extent of three and one-half million pounds per month, making a total of 42,345,461 pounds. It was this figure that the Minister of Agriculture used in his reply to the hon. member for Souris. The remainder of the oleomargarine either went into increased consumption or took the place of lard or shortening.
There were other questions asked by the hon. member for Brant-Wentworth (Mr. Charlton). Unfortunately I have not received yesterday's Hansard yet, and I am not sure of the exact questions. I will try to answer them later.

Is there any duplication in the work carried out by the laboratory of hygiene and that carried out by the provincial public health laboratories?

Questions

No. The laboratory of hygiene provides special services to the provincial laboratories which they are unable to supply for themselves, that is, investigation of outbreaks of virus diseases, laboratory diagnosis of virus infections, et cetera.
The provincial laboratories conduct certain routine diagnostic tests on specimens which, though primarily the responsibility of the federal government, would be difficult, if not impossible, to ship to the laboratory of hygiene.
Any possibility of duplication is prevented by the close collaboration and consultation afforded by the technical advisory committee on public health laboratory services. This committee is composed of the director of each provincial laboratory and representatives from the Department of Veterans Affairs and the Department of National Defence, under the chairmanship of the chief, laboratory of hygiene, together with technical consultants as required.

speechtext: To what extent does Canada follow the United States, the United Kingdom and the international civil aviation organization in the system of selection of civil pilots from the point of view of physical and mental fitness to assume flying duties?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
While the Department of
Transport is charged with the actual licensing of all civil pilots, the Department of National Health and Welfare advises, by a set medical examination, on the physical fitness of all civil pilot licence holders. Through the Department of National Health and Welfare the civil pilot medical examiners are kept up to date on new advances and requirements in aviation medicine and are given a brief but intensive course in the theory and practice of aviation medicine. Physical fitness standards for civil pilots in Canada are no less strict than those in the United Kingdom and the United States, but are probably more effectively administered as Canada is the only country that has yet given training in aviation medicine to civil pilot medical examiners.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when this debate was adjourned last evening I had pointed out that in addition to the powers conferred by the continuation of the wartime leasehold regulations, which were known as P.C. 9029, very wide powers were carried forward by the continuation of P.C. 8528. I further pointed out that those continuing powers went far beyond the continuation of the board that is necessary for the administration of the rent control regulations and that the continuation of this order provides authority to deal with most of the activities of our people in this country, including their personal services. Last night I said also that it was possible for the government to remove any uncertainty, because the government could, by order in council, revoke any part of P.C. 8528 which is not necessary for carrying on the rent control provisions.
I believe such a provision is contained in the act to which assent was given on May 14, 1947. In section 4 of that act we find these words:
The governor in council may revoke in whole or in part any order or regulation continued in force by or made under this act.
Other hon. members have put forward the argument, as I have, Mr. Speaker, that we should not be dealing with the continuation of this wartime rent control order, but rather with a rent control bill which would clearly define the rights of tenants as well as of landlords. I am sure that proposition is sound; I am sure it is consistent with our established principle of parliamentary responsibility. Nevertheless we are confronted with the inescapable fact that, by virtue of the delay of the government in presenting this measure to the house, there is now no possibility of dealing in a practical way with the alternative legislation which should have been put before us. We cannot fail to bear in mind that this control measure, unsatisfactory though it is, will terminate at midnight tomorrow night. For that reason it is certainly not my intention to oppose the passing of this bill, recognizing, as I do, that unless it is passed there will be no continuation of rent control.
Having said that, however, I do not think that the necessity for continuing the rent control measure in this unsatisfactory form should justify the continuing of measures under a wartime order in council, which places the whole of the human activity of Canada under arbitrary control if the government should choose to exercise it. Last night I expressed the hope that the government would take the simple steps necessary to remove


any uncertainty, and revoke every part of that order except the part which sets up the board. It is still possible for the government to follow that course before this bill receives final reading.
Many hon. members do not seem to believe there is any occasion to question the existence of wide powers such as these. They seem to feel that until something has actually been done under orders of this kind, there is no reason for anyone to be greatly exercised about them. Merely by way of illustration, Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out something that has recently been done under other powers, which illustrates the danger of permitting the government to use these loose powers for other purposes than those which were intended.
Doubtless every member of this house has seen reports in the press to the effect that a number of Canadians have been recently denied the use of the mails. This is a matter of greater significance than may appear on the surface. An explanation of what had happened was given by Mr. Turnbull, the deputy postmaster general. The explanation was as follows: Complaints had been received that certain people were using the mail for the purpose of soliciting the purchase of securities of various kinds. According to press reports, Mr. Turnbull explained that upon receiving complaints and examining these circulars, which related to oil development in Alberta, inspectors had been dispatched to examine the properties described. If it was found that what they saw at the property did not conform with the description in the circulars, the department took the step of denying the use of the mail to the people who had been sending those circulars.
This raises an extremely important issue, Mr. Speaker. It is clearly illustrative of the dangers of loose powers of this kind. In effect, what is being done by the postal authorities is the setting up of a securities commission in Ottawa, without any member of this house having given approval to that course. Do not let anyone suggest I am in any way seeking to prevent most effective steps being taken to restrain those who would sell securities, or anything else, by improper methods, or by circulars containing, information which does not conform with the facts. But let us see exactly what has happened in this case. Someone has complained that the circulars do not correctly describe the properties or the ventures in relation to which securities are offered to the public. Then, acting as though it were a securities commission, the Post Office Department sends someone to ascertain whether, in his

opinion, the property actually is in accordance with the description. The reason that this practice is so objectionable, Mr. Speaker, is this. There are laws dealing with matters of that kind. The Criminal Code clearly provides severe penalties for the use of circulars which improperly describe a property or ventures in relation to which securities are offered to the public. If circulars have been issued which do not correctly describe the properties or ventures which are referred to, and are therefore misleading the public, charges should be laid under the Criminal Code. I think every hon. member in this house would hope that charges would be laid. In my own opinion, charges are long overdue in regard to a number of the circulars which have been issued with respect to certain properties. But no member of this house has been called upon to say what kind of securities commission he wants set up. No member of this house has been asked to express his opinion as to how wide those powers should be. No member of this house has been told how a securities commission in Ottawa is going to relate its activities to those of securities commissions in the provinces. In fact, no member of this house and no member of parliament has authorized the Post Office Department or any other department to act in this way.

I am giving this information which, I admit, may not greatly help the parliamentary assistant, because it is quite obvious that he has not informed himself- or had not up until last night-in regard to the legislation which is before us. It is for this reason that I am hoping that, by an illustration of this kind, hon. members may be made aware of the dangers of loose powers exercised without the authority of parliament.
I return to the illustration I was giving. Since this is a current illustration, it should be the very kind that would help hon. members to understand why we should be exceed-
Transitional Measures Act ingly careful to see to it that the authority of parliament is respected. I think it must be of some interest to hon. members that these orders restraining the use of the mails by certain Canadians happened to coincide with similar orders made in the United States; it seemed to be a remarkable coincidence that our Post Office Department had acted at the same time as the United States, and in relation to the same people.
So far as I am aware, this parliament has not yet authorized anyone to act under instructions of the securities exchange commission in the United States; and I hope the time will not come when this parliament will ever authorize any Canadian official so to do. By all means let us co-operate to the very limit in preventing the issue of fraudulent circulars or fraudulent documents of any kind. But let us remember that in the United States there are procedures which have no place in this country under our legal system. Let us remember that the United States have a practice of issuing in a loose way orders which deny certain rights to citizens and which do not bear any resemblance to any procedure we have. In Canada we insist that our citizens be able to have their rights determined before the courts. In this particular case the Post Office Department, doubtless believing that it is acting in the best interests of the public, is exercising powers which were never extended intentionally by parliament, and is doing indirectly something that I am convinced parliament would not authorize.
I give that illustration because it indicates exactly the sort of thing that can happen under the wide powers granted and continued under this act, not in relation to rent controls but in relation to other matters-in relation to the control of personal services, the handling of goods, and other activities. I can only repeat that the government should not leave these powers in such a position that they can be put into effect by anyone and that Canadians may find themselves being dealt with under a procedure which denies to them the ordinary access to the courts.
I am not going to introduce an amendment, for the simple reason that, because of this confused procedure being followed by the government, we are dealing with an act which merely continues an order in council that could be revoked this afternoon. Consequently it is almost impossible, from the practical point of view, to deal with this particular subject. It is like dealing with quicksilver. This afternoon we might introduce an amendment dealing with a particular aspect of this matter, and it could be disposed of by order in council, as it should be. I present

Transitional Measures Act these arguments merely in the hope that the government, before this bill is finally dealt with, will remove from this continuing P.C. 8528 all those powers which do not actually relate to the setting up of the board which is necessary for rent controls.

shall not detain the house for more than a few minutes, Mr. Speaker. For reasons that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) gave in his speech yesterday, and for some of the reasons which the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) has placed before the house today, I believe that we should be considering a statute in which the powers relating to rent control would be clearly set out. Nevertheless, for the reasons the leader of the opposition gave a few moments ago, and because of the pressure of time-although there is still time for the government to reconsider its position in this respect-we propose to vote for the bill as introduced.
What I really rose to do, sir, was to pursue a question that I asked this afternoon of the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters), because it comes under the head of housing accommodation and rent controls. I have now a more complete written answer from the minister, which was handed to me a moment ago by a page boy, upon which I wish to make one or two comments. After all, rent control is a minor matter when we consider the need for housing accommodation. In his answer to the question I asked today with regard to the eviction from 50 Argyle avenue in this city of some fifty families and one hundred children, the minister said that the responsibility for the administration of emergency housing at 50 Argyle avenue, which was erected during the war on real property leased to the crown by a petroleum company, is in the hands of the city of Ottawa. What I wish to do is to comment on the part of the answer that the minister did not read, and which states:
At the conclusion of hostilities the Argyle barracks was leased by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to the city of Ottawa for use as an emergency shelter accommodation.
Consequently it appears that this property was leased by the crown during the war and again was leased after the war by a crown organization, namely, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. What I am anxious to find, out is how long this lease lasted; is it still in effect; and why, in view of the rental and housing conditions in this city, a piece of property housing fifty families is being returned to a petroleum company which, according to the information I have, merely desires to turn it into a parking place for automobiles. It seems to me that the need of

the people to park themselves and their children is much more urgent than the parking of automobiles.
I appeal to the government to look into this matter, to reconsider it, and to see that while the housing shortage lasts in this city, both emergency accommodation of this kind and ordinary accommodation for rent are made available to hard-pressed families and not handed over to a petroleum company for the parking of automobiles.

Transitional Measures Act and were used, as the hon. member will recall, with great effect.
The second thing I want to say is this: This kind of treatment is part of a pattern that we are growing used to. I give one illustration; it has been in my mind ever since it happened, and I shall never have a better opportunity to get it off my mind than now. When this house opened in February the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), in a nonchalant way, undertook to invade one of the traditional privileges of this house, namely, the priority of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. The leader of the opposition, in what I thought was a quiet, cogent, well reasoned speech, suggested that he should not have done that. In the course of his speech he also quoted some cogent phrases from the former prime minister of this country, whose opinion at one time was highly regarded by hon. gentlemen on the opposite side of the house.
I am not really complaining primarily that the views of the leader of the opposition, or of the former prime minister of Canada, were not followed; what I am complaining about is that that argument was not answered. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this is part of a pattern; that is the kind of thing that we are getting used to in this house, and apparently we have to go on being used to it as long as there is this huge majority which will vote right. The only other thing I have to say is that I am very sorry I had to make this speech without the benefit of hearing the speech of the member for Coast-Capilano. I presume we shall now hear from him.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
May I tell my hon. friend that I spent all morning reading his many speeches, all really the same speech, but I shall come back to him in ten or fifteen minutes. The first thing I should like to do is to speak to the bill which is now before us. I should like to give a short history and some reasons why after eight years we are asking for the last thirteen months continuation of the few measures which are still in effect.
This bill really stems back to the War Measures Act which was passed in 1914 by the Borden government. That was a most necessary measure and gave the government of that day wide powers and the ability to act speedily and with flexibility on the very grave and pressing problems which occur in wartime. Then at the end of the war, in 1918, the Conservative government of that day did not repeal the War Measures Act, but continued to use it-it was a matter of


judgment-to enable them to hurdle the transitional period which always comes after the end of every war. The War Measures Act remained on the books then for 20 years and it was again made effective on September 1, 1939, when a state of war with the German reich was declared by this government although the actual declaration of war awaited action by parliament.
Looking back I think it was very useful that the War Measures Act had remained on the statute books of Canada for that period. The government of the day had the power to take action quickly. Under the War Measures Act as it was reinvoked in September, 1939, the government had wide powers to deal with the many emergencies which promptly arose. One of the first, of course, was the great dislocation in the ordinary economy of this country caused mainly by the artificial shortages which had occurred from the channelling of labour into the armed services and into war industries which resulted in shortages of materials and supplies. Therefore, it was necessary to impose controls which we would normally regard as unjustifiable in a free economy, controls to ensure that our economy would remain on an even balance, controls to ensure that everyone in this country would have a fair share at a fair price of what goods there were.
I think the system of price control built up by the Right Hon. J. L. Ilsley and administered by Mr. Donald Gordon was the -best in the world and it certainly won the admiration of the Canadian people; not perhaps all those who are professional politicians, but the little people of Canada who were protected by these controls.
In 1945 the Liberal government of that day, unlike the Conservative government of 1919, did not continue in effect the War Measures Act. On the other hand, they said that the time had come to come back to parliament for further authority, which they did in the fall session of 1945 after winning a really democratic vote of confidence of the people of Canada in their conduct of measures like this. I should like to read the preamble to the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, as follows:
And whereas during the national emergency arising by reason of the war against Germany and Japan measures have been adopted under the War Measures Act for the military requirements and security of Canada and the maintenance of economic stability; and whereas the national emergency arising out of the war has continued since the unconditional surrender of Germany and Japan and is still continuing; and whereas it is essential in the national interest that certain transitional powers continue to be exercisable by the governor in council during the continuation of the exceptional conditions brought about by the war-

This is the important part of the statement: -and it is preferable that such transitional powers be exercised hereafter under special authority in that behalf conferred by parliament instead of being exercised under the War Measures Act;
So we had the first of the transitional powers acts coming forward, as hon. members who were here will recall, in the fall session of 1945. It extended the powers for one year because even then the government was hopeful that the transitional period would pass quickly and did not ask for any longer extension of time. By 1946 conditions had improved to some extent as far as the free flow of goods was concerned and added relaxations were possible. A further extension was needed and the government of the day came to parliament and asked for an extension of one year.
Then in 1947 a large-scale revision was made. We were then two years away from the war. The hundreds of orders in council and directives which were in force during the war were reduced to fifty-seven and they were appended as a schedule to the bill. There was discussion in parliament at that time on every one of those orders in council and because of the action of members of parliament the number was cut from fifty-seven to fifty. When some hon. members say loosely that parliament has not seen these orders in council, may I remind them that every one passed in detail through this house as a schedule to the bill of 1947. The only changes made since that time in any of those orders have been by means of amending orders to restrict the powers given to the government under that bill.
In 1948 a further revision was made and there was an extension of time again for a year. Most of the wartime controls had now gone by the board. At that time the Conservatives were saying that we were too slow and should do what the United States was doing and eliminate most of the controls. At the same time the C.C.F. members were crying that we were going too fast, that we should hold on to the controls. We took the middle course and once again the people of Canada showed their approval of that course in the general election of 1949.
In 1949 we came and asked for one more year. At that time the hundreds of wartime orders in council which had dropped to fifty in 1947 was down to twelve. We asked for a time extension until March 31 of this year. This whittling-down process of controls and rationing continued as goods came into ample supply on the market.
We now come back to parliament in 1950. Last week the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) stood in his place and told parliament that this would be the last time extension we would ask for. This bill provides for a thirteen months extension to end the few
Transitional Measures Act controls which are now in effect. More than that, the number of orders in council is to be cut to six after April 1. We are in sight of the end of our policy of orderly decontrol.
The people of Canada realize this. The change in this country has been quite uniform. Some people may say that certain controls were taken off too rapidly, but in looking back at the whole picture I think that we have conducted our policy of orderly decontrol, trying to get back to the old free relations between buyer and seller, in sound fashion.
Both the putting on of controls and the carrying on of orderly decontrols took courage. The people of Canada have often paid tribute to the great courage and the high integrity shown by the Right Hon. J. L. Ilsley and Mr. Donald Gordon in the matter of building up and administrating the wartime prices and trade board which did this great job. I do not think that enough recognition has been paid to the less glamorous but equally difficult job which has been done by the present Minister of Finance and Mr. K. W. Taylor in carrying out our decontrol policy. Today we have cut down from 6,000 employees, which was the peak, and many hundreds of orders in council, to the present six orders in council and 750 employees, of whom 500 are in rental control in the field and 250 are dealing with rental control problems and in the import quota branch here in Ottawa.
Another interesting thing has been the great change-in the attitude in the house toward this matter. Only five hon. members in all have spoken on the two stages of the resolution and on the motion for second reading of this bill, and since last Friday the department with which I am associated has received not one single letter as a consequence of the announcement on decontrol then made by the Minister of Finance. Hon. members will recall that when previous controls were taken off alarms were stirred up in this house and it was said that the government had lost the confidence of the people. That is what happened at the end of every rationing or other control. Yet six months later things had levelled off and the country had taken one step more back to what we regarded before the war as being a free economy, and members had forgotten their original unfounded fears.
I can remember being alarmed myself once and how I caused quite a bit of trouble to the minister in connection with the decontrol of commercial accommodation which occurred a year and a half ago. I was sure that that was a most premature step, and spoke strongly against it. Yet as a consequence of this action, within six months new office buildings had been built across the country and good space was available. Landlords who had been
1356

Transitional Measures Act getting exorbitant rents for old space because nobody was building new space or stores were having their rents hammered down to what they should be as decent space became available. Today we hear no demand across the country for a return to commercial rental controls.
I finish by saying that all this bill is is a last step in this eight-year program of necessary economic control which was a consequence of vur entry into the war. Each year since 1945 we have been whittling away at these orders in council. It is true that we had great powers under the War Measures Act; it is true that we had the considerable powers given to us in the first transitional powers act of 1945; but these powers are now almost all gone and twice since that time we have gone to the real court of last resort, the people of Canada, for an indication of approval of those policies, in 1945 and 1949. I want to tell hon. members-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: A minority vote both times.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: -that there is no part of the entire government program which came closer home to the little people of Canada, the people of my constituency because I represent an industrial riding, the worker and his wife who are trying to raise a family. It is these people whose confidence in this government's policies was responsible for the return of the government with the greatest majority since confederation, for the reduction of the Conservative party and the almost total obliteration of the C.C.F.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: A minority vote both times.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I know the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is most anxious to get on his feet. In my notes, which I am sure the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) will concede I did not write in the moment or two he was speaking, my next heading is "Knowles". I must start off by making an apology to the hon. member which I hope he will take in good faith. I have already spoken to him privately on the matter. The other evening when the minister handed me the bill there was attached to it a mimeographed sheet from the privy council office headed "Schedule to the act". After all, as the hon. member for Greenwood pointed out, I am not a lawyer and I naturally assumed it was the schedule to the bill now before the house. It is actually what remains of the effective schedule to the act of 1947. In past years the courtesy has been extended of having the actual remaining orders in council placed on Hansard. I thought I was also extending a courtesy although it has not been very gratefully received by the hon. member. I want to point out, however-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Just a minute. I am quite prepared to accept in good faith the apology the hon. member is making, but he had better make it in good faith and admit that he did not just say the other night he would place it on Hansard but that it would be a schedule to the bill.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit one comment? I want to make it perfectly clear that the only thing I had in mind was that the parliamentary assistant last night undertook to answer a purely legal question. I am not sneering at all at his knowledge of the general situation. My comment was directed to the fact that he undertook to disagree with competent lawyers on a purely legal question.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The hon. member has misunderstood the point I am making. Last night, in commenting on what the hon. member for

Winnipeg North Centre had said, the hon. member for Greenwood said that often the officials in the rental offices do not know all the law. I am pointing out that if everybody in Canada knew all the law, certainly if the ordinary layman could pick it all up from the law books, read them and understand them, there would be no business for lawyers, and that might be a good thing for Canada.
The next point made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was that the people of the country are going to be left high and dry in 1951 with the end of federal rent control. I should like to remind him that the problem of rent control can be properly handled by the provinces, and I was going to say his own province, but the province of his heart's desire, Saskatchewan, has taken such action.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Tell me what they do in my own province of Manitoba.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I want to say more than that. If further decontrol is necessary over the next thirteen months then the bodies which can do it best are those governments which are closest to the people, the provincial governments. In my own riding of Coast-Capilano there are two areas, north Vancouver and west Vancouver, where rental control is certainly still necessary, but there is a great area from Horseshoe bay to Powell river where there is no need for rent control today. After all, the provincial governments are closer to the people and to local problems, and if they desire to do so next spring they can move into the field and perhaps institute the process which is the reverse of the one we have commenced, that of partial decontrol, only in the necessary areas.
The hon. member also mentioned the complexity of these orders in council and he reeled them off. Actually the whole trend is the other way. Not one of the amending orders in council which I put on Hansard, no amending order after 1945, was an expanding order. Every one was an order stripping away and restricting power. Therefore, rather than being more and more complex, these orders are continually diminishing. Of course that is the whole intent of the policy of orderly decontrol. Finally he asked-and I think rather naively-why we did not put the whole thing in one act in simple language that every layman would understand. It may be heresy, but I had to consult a legal authority on this question. He immediately pointed out that today the whole problem is not entirely our problem. It is complicated by the landlord and tenant laws of every province, and even if we had the right to do so we could not produce a simple understandable law effective in every province which every 55946-87J
Transitional Measures Act [DOT]layman would immediately know designated his rights as to the entire matter of rents. As-I pointed out, every tenant who is affected by these orders in council today has been affected for at least three years, and most of them for eight years. They certainly know their rights, and they know where to go if they need further information.
Let me turn to the remarks of the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming). I hope he will pardon me if I do not spend very much time on them for the reason that we have heard the same speech for the last four years. I did not quite realize how similar his remarks were until I spent this morning in. the library thumbing through the debates on this measure in 1945, 1946, 1947, 1948 and 1949. I picked out a few of his words which he has used in every speech, lovely words such as "centralization", "dictatorship", "bureaucratic invasion", "unwarranted invasion of provincial rights", "sweeping totalitarian powers", and this lovely one, "assassination of the constitution". The funny thing is that when the hon. member works himself into a frenzy of indignation in the house he is never amusing, but it is very amusing to sit in the quiet of the library four years afterwards and read how the act of 1945 was going to' assassinate the Canadian constitution.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Which 1945 act do you mean, the act that was passed or the bill that the government introduced and then withdrew under a storm of protest?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Let me turn to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew). I take considerable pleasure in analysing his remarks. I notice that he is busy writing but I know he is also listening. His was the old, old thesis that we have heard so often in the short time he has been in the house. He says that what we are doing is the right thing but we are doing it in the wrong way. I am sorry that we have not all received yesterday's Hansard, but I have the manuscript. Last night the leader of the opposition said there was no disagreement about the purpose of the things we are doing, and then he went on to sayr
But there should be disagreement on the part of every member of this house with the procedure-that is being followed . . .
Let us look at the procedure now and see-whether we are doing the right thing but in the wrong way. He makes his usual tacit assumption of course that the only right way to do anything in Canada is the way George Drew wants it done. The people of High Park and the people of Canada showed most distinctly that they do not want things done the way George Drew wants to do them, but do want things done the way this government has done them since 1935. His suggestion at
1358	HOUSE OF
Transitional Measures Act this time is that what we need is a new bill, a complete bill covering the present rental control, so everything will be clearly stated, in orderly language. He wants a new act of parliament. I am going to refer to a legal authority, and I hope the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) is listening. This is not the Department of Justice, but an authority that I am sure even he will respect. It is the Supreme Court of Canada, which passed on this very problem by reference on March 24, 1950. The opening clause of the judgment, of course, is familiar to all. The chief justice said:
There is no doubt that under normal conditions the subject matter of rents belongs to the provincial jurisdiction under the head of property and civil rights, in section 92 of the British North America Act.
Then he goes on and discusses various leading cases, and then comes to the summation of his opinion and that of the other justices:
.... in the circumstances, this court may not doubt that parliament may competently . . .
Then listen to these words:
. . . maintain the regulations it has adopted to meet the emergency and its continuance.
Notice the words "maintain the regulations".
And listen to this:
Therefore the wartime leasehold regulations are not ultra vires either in whole or in part.
Again, that is the present regulations Which have worked so well for the last eight years.
Suppose at this eleventh hour, after eight years of satisfactory administration under this series of acts, we had brought in a new act this session. Hon. members on this side of the house and in the other corner know what would have happened. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) would have risen and thundered with all his eloquence that here the shilly-shallying government had changed its mind at the eleventh hour. He would ask, what was wrong with the old way? It had done well for years. But the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) would be in a much better position; after five years he would have something new in his speech. He would say we are not only deceiving the people of Canada, we are not only deceiving the parliament of Canada, but now we have tricked the supreme court because we gave them one set of regulations and as soon as they said they were intra vires we whipped in here and passed a new bill, which would be permanent.
I think it is necessary to have a return to reality, a return to the people of Canada. The laws of this country are not made for


lawyers; they are made to serve the people. The people have been well served by the policies of the wartime prices and trade board since 1941, operating under this act. The people know the policy of this government has been one of orderly decontrol, and it has been successfully carried out. The people know also that we are rounding out that policy, and this bill is now only asking for an extension for thirteen months of these six remaining effective orders. If the Conservative party wants to delay the passage of this bill beyond tomorrow night, and end all rent control, the people of Canada will know that, too.

Will the parliamentary
assisfant give us more information, or at least clarify the information he gave us during his oration a few moments ago, in regard to the number still in the employ of the wartime prices and trade board. maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is my information.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Then I take it there are no employees who could administer any of these sections in the wartime prices and trade orders in council that are being carried forward in dead letter form? .

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
This is perhaps not relevant to the section, but I am glad to give the information. One reason everything does not relate solely to rents is the fact that we still have a few carry-overs, such as appeals and convictions, under the prices board. Under the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation there are some appeals from the refusal of subsidies, and some of the employees-not across Canada, but here in Ottawa-are still engaged in that work.

That is why it was necessary to carry forward those orders, not to impose new controls or grant new subsidies but to clean up the odds and ends of that work that still remain.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: There was one other question. In replying to my remarks the parliamentary assistant dealt with the argument I had put forward that an attempt should be made to put into this statute a boiled-down form of the law as it now stands with respect to rent control. It seemed to me that he argued two ways. On the one hand he argued that it was too complex to put into a statute, and on the other hand he told me that most of the subsequent orders in council and board orders had been for the purpose of lessening the regulation and control and thus making the situation more simple. If his latter argument is so, surely it would be a simple matter to put it into statutory form. He knows as well as I do-and both of us may be grateful that we are not lawyers-that there are such things as office consolidations. In fact office consolidations are in existence now as far as these rental regulations are concerned. There is an office consolidation of P.C. 9029, which is the basic rent control order in council. That office consolidation sets out P.C. 9029 in the form in which it would be if you worked into it all the subsequent amendments. Board order 800, which I believe is the basic board order with respect to rent control, has been amended by subsequent board orders, and there is in existence an office consolidation of that. I am not suggesting it is necessary to change the rent control law to bring in something different from what was approved by the supreme court, but would it not be possible to produce what in effect would be an office consolidation of the law as it now stands and write that into this statute so people could see exactly what the law is?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I cannot add anything to the argument I made. My argument on the complexity of the rental law was based on the fact that we have ten provinces with different landlord and tenant laws which also would be involved in any complete analysis for a layman.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is the situation now.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
That brings me to my last point. For the last three years the tenants and landlords of Canada have been working under these very regulations. Why should we, in the last thirteen months, go to the expense, if you will, or have the innovation of introducing a further consolidation? If this were an expanding control of course we would do that, but it is a control that has been constantly whittled down so that now it consists of only
Transitional Measures Act six orders, all of them now in effect and all well known to the people who have been affected by them for the last three years. Neither I nor the members of the government can see any real purpose that would be served.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The parliamentary assistant and I represent constituencies in which there are areas where rent control is of concern to the people. He says that is so in only part of his constituency, but it affects the people in all parts of my riding. In view of the fact that the federal government is going out of this field in 13 months, does the parliamentary assistant recommend that his provincial government in British Columbia and the provincial government in my province of Manitoba get ready to take over the matter?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, there is an excellent rule about minding your own business. I believe that is the course I would follow so far as the provincial government of British Columbia is concerned. The hon. member can govern himself accordingly.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Is the hon. member saying that he minds his own business so far as the provincial government of British Columbia is concerned?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I certainly do.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I thought he fathered it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: You never saw me on a coalition platform.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I should like to bring the parliamentary assistant back to some of the simple aspects of the argument advanced by the leader of the opposition and myself last night, and which the parliamentary assistant has completely overlooked today.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, we have been through the resolution stage and second reading of this bill. On this clause, he has not the right once again to wander over the entire field, and give us the latest version of this four-year old speech.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The hon. member must direct his remarks to the clause under consideration.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
That is precisely what I am doing, Mr. Chairman. While the parliamentary assistant was putting on this interesting matinee performance, he ignored the fact that unnecessary but very sweeping powers continue, and that statutory effect

Transitional Measures Act will be given to those orders in council. He has said that these six orders in council are part of the schedule to the 1947 act. One does not find the text of them there, so he was completely astray of the mark.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: There is a list of them there.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: So what?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
If my friend can restrain himself, with effort, for a moment, then we shall get on with this problem. I should like to put some questions to the parliamentary assistant designed to elicit from him such information as may be in his possession. The effect of the section now under consideration will be to extend, for a period of thirteen months, this Transitional Measures Act. Will the parliamentary assistant turn to this important and sweeping order P.C. 8528, which was passed to meet the war emergency when it was at its height. I am going to invite him to direct his attention to section 4 of the order, subsection (1), paragraph (a):
4. (1) The board shall have power
(a) to investigate, of Its own motion or on complaint, costs, prices, profits and stocks of goods and materials of any person engaged in the manufacture, importation, exportation, production, storage, transportation, supply or sale of any goods or services or any alleged or apparent offence under these regulations, and for the purpose of any such investigation the board shall have all the powers of a commissioner appointed under the provisions of the Inquiries Act;

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Will the hon. member repeat the section?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Section 4 (1) (a) of order 8528, appearing on page 22 of the consolidation that was used in 1947, but is not part of the statute.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am informed that this is actually the section to which I referred in my speech, and to which I referred in answering the member for Winnipeg North Centre. maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

To enter any premises and to inspect and examine any or all books, records and stocks of goods and materials in the possession or control of any person and to require any such person to produce such books and records at any place before it or before any person appointed by it to investigate, and to take possession of and remove any or all such books and records;

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Again, a very interesting answer, read in the light of the statement made in this house by the minister last Friday which can be found at page 1089 of Hansard, March 24. He said:
Therefore the practical effect of the proposed bill is to continue the authority to control rentals only, for a further period.

powers besides rent control that the government is proposing to retain in favour of the wartime prices and trade board. Let me read paragraph (c):

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Where is that found?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
At page 1089 of Hansard. The minister said:
Therefore the practical effect of the proposed bill Is to continue the authority to control rentals only, . . .

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Where does he mention them?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Not controls on prices, not added subsidies, but to finish up the payment of these few challenged subsidies which are now outstanding.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I challenge the parliamentary assistant to point out any place in the speech the minister made last Friday where he said anything about its being necessary to clean up the odds and ends of price control. Earlier in the same paragraph of the minister's speech, we find this;
While no other change is proposed, I should state that during the past year all the orders contained in the schedule to the act have been revoked except those relating to price and rent control. The government does not intend to invoke the limited powers now granted by the act to reimpose controls already lifted. Therefore the practical effect of the proposed' bill is to continue the authority to control rentals only, for a further period.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The practical effect.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: What does price control mean?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I fail to see the possible relevancy of that question to the matter before us, when the minister has said that the practical effect is to continue the authority to control rentals only. Surely that is quite enough. But apparently that was one of those mere statements of intention by

There are one or two questions that I should like to ask the parliamentary assistant. They have to do with the submission made to the Supreme Court of Canada in reference to the continuance of emergency powers. The judgment delivered by the Supreme Court of Canada was one of the most striking ever delivered. It is one that peculiarly affects the constitutional set-up of this country. I say that because it is the first judgment on so important a matter passed by the supreme court since it became the supreme court. I use the word "judgment" advisedly, even though the chief justice properly pointed out that what the court was in fact doing was merely answering a question submitted to it as to whether or not the emergency powers in connection with rental control were continuing, and as such were within the jurisdiction of the federal parliament.
I want to find out first whether any appeal has been launched against the submission and

Transitional Measures Act the answers given by the supreme court. Second, if an appeal has been launched, by whom has it been launched, and in the normal course of events when will it be heard? This happens to be one of these matters that niay still be appealed to the privy council. At the moment I am asking for information as to whether or not the privy council is going to deal with this matter.
No judgment has been handed down in years that indicates and emphasizes the responsibilities of the federal parliament as does this submission or reference which I am discussing; for in effect it says, as I interpret it, that when and if parliament declares the existence of an emergency, arising out of either war or insurrection, or in any other manner whatsoever, then the court will be bound to agree, unless there is very strong evidence to the contrary, that parliament had the right to invade the jurisdiction of the provinces.
As I understand the import of the judgment, it means that if we in parliament make the declaration, irrespective of the provisions of the British North America Act with regard to division of powers under sections 91 and 92, the court will be most loath not to uphold the declaration of emergency. It is the judgment on the reference which indicates just how far this parliament could go in invading provincial rights, unless the House of Commons and the Senate were most careful to ensure that there was in fact an emergency before making such a declaration in the preamble.
I notice that the parliamentary assistant pointed in the general direction of the Minister of Justice. I feel sure that the Minister of Justice will make some extended reference to this submission, which is one of the most outstanding in Canadian constitutional history.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, dealing with the first point raised by the hon. member for Lake Centre, may I say that, so far as we in the Department of Justice are aware, up to date no appeal has been entered against the judgment in question.
With regard to the other observations made by my hon. and learned friend, I would very much prefer not to deal with a matter of this importance in the extemporaneous manner'in which it has been raised today. But I think I should say that the point which the hon. member makes is not borne out by all of the judgments of the judges of the supreme court. Just taking at random from the judgments which I sent for only a

few moments ago, when this matter seemed to be imminent, Mr. Justice Taschereau states in his judgment:
In the present instance,-
That is, in the case referred to the court.
-no evidence of any kind has been submitted to show that the emergency had disappeared and that normal conditions are now prevailing. On the contrary, common knowledge, to which it is surely permissible to appeal in a case of this kind, and the very valuable exhibits in the record which I have usefully consulted to test the accuracy of the statements, lead me to the irresistible conclusion that an emergency still exists as an aftermath of the war.
That is a judicial finding, not a legislative assertion, of an emergency. Then I quote again from page 13 of the multigraphed copy of the judgment as follows:
It follows that if there is unmistakable evidence to make it clear that there is no emergency, the courts are duty bound to intervene.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Is that still Mr. Justice Taschereau?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Yes. He continues:
Otherwise, we would reach a conclusion that is not justified by the British North America Act. Under the guise of "Peace, order and good government," it would be possible for the parliament of Canada to enact colourable legislation, and wrongly assume powers that belong to the provincial legislatures. Confederation has been erected on more solid foundations.
But such is not the case. The war has created an emergency that justified the governor general in council to bring the War Measures Act in operation and pass regulations to meet such an emergency. Parliament then enacted the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act (1945) and the Continuation of Transitional Measures Act (1947) because in its opinion the emergency that arose out of the war was still existing, and for the express purpose of decontrolling, and to complete the orderly transition from abnormal to normal conditions.
The regulations that were passed to reach that aim are essentially of a temporary character, and the laws from which they derive their validity are in no way permanent. They will come to an end with the emergency.
I mention that judgment simply to indicate that it is rather dangerous to generalize in the way in which I understood my hon. and learned friend did as to the nature of the judgment. I think I am right in saying that a judgment was delivered by every one of the judges who sat on the case and necessarily the reasons were not all the same. Reasons were given by Mr. Justice Taschereau to the effect that if there were a clear case of parliament attempting to declare, as a foundation for its jurisdiction, an emergency which did not in fact exist, then the jurisdiction would not stand.

But, Mr. Speaker, although we do not know exactly all that we are going to do, we know exactly what we are not going to do; that is, we are not going to let the prices fall to the low levels to which they fell in 1920, and again in 1932, 1933, 1934 and a few other years.

First there is, under section 9, subsection 1(a) and (b),-

The feature of the deficiency payment is that under this scheme there is no* interference with the natural fluctuations of price brought about by the laws of supply and demand. If that average price is deemed to be too low to support and reasonably maintain production, the board, with the approval of the governor in council, sets a value on the unit commodity which in its judgment will bring sufficient return at this price to the producer . . .
Further down on page 5801 the minister said:
This is the policy of the bill. At the end of the year, as I said, there would be a calculation made as to the average price, and if the unit commodity has been sold below that average price the difference is paid between the average price and the price at which it should have been to give a fair return to all those who have sold this commodity.
