Manitoba fishermen had thereby sold less than half their last year's quantities. The surplus fish was threatened with spoilage, unless action was taken to buy and move it from the lakes into cold storage warehouses in Winnipeg.
A few days later the Department of Fisheries said they would buy 5 million pounds of frozen fish, including whitefish, saugers, pike, pickerel, trout and tullibee, at prices approximately 80 per cent of the going price for frozen fish. I do not object to that; that is all right. Further down in the report it is said that this price would be paid at the cold storage warehouses in Winnipeg. At that stage, the fish have passed into the hands of the packer, who can pay anything he likes for the fish to the man we are trying to help. I object to that. I want to see the primary producer get the benefit of this good legislation which has been put on the order paper, not the packer, who can look after himself quite well.
I said before that I supported this bill last time, and I am going to support it again. I should like to move an amendment-
Mr. MacN aught: I do not like to interrupt the hon. member, but I think he is creating a wrong impression. All the cheques for those fish went to the individual fishermen, and not to the packers.
I do not think that is right, sir. I know that all the packing companies that held fish were paid for the fish. This money was not paid to the man who caught the fish up at Norway House-
Perhaps they were on consignment.

They were only partly consigned, Mr. Lumberman. When I asked about this matter, the return I was given showed where the money was paid, and where the fish went. They went to Canada Packers at a cent a pound to be made into fish meal.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: That is where the fish went after they were bought.

Yes, but the packers were paid for it. The fish companies in Winnipeg were paid, and I could put their names on the record. The primary producer is the man who goes out on the lake and fishes. He is the man who suffers all the hardships, and then has to take what the other fellow is willing to give him.
I am going to move an amendment, Mr. Speaker, which reads as follows:
That Bill No. 54 be not now read a second time, but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house consideration should be given to the introducing of legislation to amend the Fisheries Prices Support Act so as to provide that floor prices should be established at such levels as to guarantee to those engaged in the fishing industry a price-cost relationship not less favourable than that prevailing in the period 1944-48.
This amendment is seconded by the member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis). I believe it will improve the bill, and it is for that reason I move the amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words in support of the amendment. I do not think very much needs to be added to what has been said by the member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce). I come from a constituency on the Pacific coast in which a great many fishermen reside. The men who are engaged in taking the fish out of the sea are fairly well organized, and can generally get a fair deal with the packers and others who buy their fish. In eastern Canada I understand the fishermen are not so well organized, and are not in as good a position to get a fair share of the value of the product they help to produce.
I think we should pay attention to the point made by the member for St. John's East (Mr. Higgins) that on the east coast, where fishing is so hazardous an occupation, when the fishermen undertake to go through the hardships of bringing the fish to shore, they never know what they are going to receive for their fish. As a matter of fact, they have little control over the price they receive. Consequently, whether the fishermen participate directly or indirectly in the monetary benefits of price support, they should know before the fish are taken out of the sea what they are going to receive for their labour. As was said in the debate on the agricultural bill, it should not be left to the whim or caprice of a fisheries minister or a cabinet to decide what the price support may be.
I appreciate this bill. I see that it is to be continued for an indefinite period, but any amendment we may make now relating to the price relationship would not of course

remain permanently. It could be amended in the same way that other sections of the bill are amended, if any change took place in the cost of living. Then another period could be taken to determine the price relationship. I suggest that this amendment does not hold up the bill. The bill could be passed with the assurance that the fishermen and those engaged in that industry will know exactly what price support will mean in actual practice.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the amendment carry? Those in favour of the amendment please say yea.
Yea.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Those against will say nay.
Nay.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
In my opinion the nays have it. I declare the amendment lost.
Amendment (Mr. Bryce) negatived.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. J. Browne (St. John's West):
speechtext:
I should like to make a few observations in support of what the member for St. John's East (Mr. Higgins) has said. I represent a constituency a portion of which, outside the city of St. John's, is principally concerned with the fishing industry as a means of livelihood. In St. John's West, the principal people engaged in this trawling business are established. It must be realized that we are principally concerned about the salt codfish industry in Newfoundland. It has always been a matter of great concern to the fishermen of Newfoundland to know what price they are going to get for their fish. As my hon. friend has stated, this business being conducted on a credit basis and not on a cash basis, in the spring of the year the fisherman generally goes to a merchant, locally he is called a supply merchant, and takes on supplies. He would like to know then, not six months after that, what he is going to get for his fish. Otherwise he does not know how the price he is paying for his supplies is going to relate to the price he is going to get for his fish.
Over one hundred years ago a law was passed that made it obligatory for the merchants to set up the prices when the men went to look for supplies, so that they would know what was going to be paid for the fish; and at various times since it has been found necessary. It is certainly desirable that as soon as possible, at the earliest part of the season, in August, the fishermen should be told what the price of fish is going to be.
In our country at the present time we have a fisheries board that has been in operation for about five years. At various times we have had various measures to help the fisherman.
29. 1950
Fisheries Prices Support Act I remember in 1933 the merchants would not supply the fisherman, and the government had to come forward and give a guarantee that they would compensate the merchant if the fisherman was not able to pay for the supplies he got. I think it can be easily seen how important this business is in Newfoundland. There are 28,000 fishermen and through the various ramifications the number of people who are concerned with the successful progress of the fishing voyage is greater than that in any other industry in the province.
At the present time, in the month of March, the first fishermen begin to go to the Grand Banks from the southern portion of the island. They are engaged in trawling on the Grand Banks. As can be imagined, that is a strenuous life at this time of the year. As my hon. friend has said, it is the fishermen who go down to Labrador who are now the most concerned. In my constituency last year the chief trouble we had was that the people did not catch any fish. I do not know whether anything can be done for them except what was done by putting them on relief work initiated by the provincial government.
But as to the price of fish, of the two measures envisaged under the continuation of this act, one is that the government will buy the fish that cannot be sold. I should like the minister or his parliamentary assistant to tell us if anything will be done in Newfoundland this year with regard to that. We had some difficulty in disposing of the catch. I do not know whether it is all disposed of as yet. One of the things that saved the situation down there was that the fishing was not as great as it is normally. One of the purposes of the act is to see that there is a fair relationship between the return from the fisheries and that from other occupations. That purpose was stressed when the bill was introduced in 1944 and I hope it will be kept in mind for the future.
Last year the minister, speaking with regard to the fisheries, told us that he was going to set up three committees, I believe: one dealing with marketing, one dealing with technical services, and one dealing with consumers' services. I do not know whether he has been able to make any progress in this matter since then; but if he has been able to do so, I hope he will tell us what he has done.
The hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. Higgins) has pointed out the situation with regard to the Labrador fishermen, and in some respects what he said applied to other fishermen. It is desirable for them to know the price. That is why it is important that a floor should be set under the price of fish. It is important for them to know at as

Fisheries Prices Support Act early a date as possible what is going to be paid for the fish, so that they will know whether it is worth while for them to go into it or not.
I do not intend to speak at any length. I just want to refer to this point. The amendment that was moved here, it seems to me, would not suit at the present time because there has been a decline in the price of fish and the fishermen have had to accept a lower price for fish than they were getting up to last year. But nevertheless there is a point beyond which we cannot allow the price of fish to go or, as in the case of the Labrador men, they will have to give up the fishery and they will not be able to go down there at all. The same thing may apply to the shore fishery. I am sure that the intention of this act is to prevent a large body of people from being put out of employment. I hope the minister will be able to give us some information on these matters.

I just wish to make a few brief remarks in connection with this resolution. I believe that I am perhaps as greatly interested in the fishing industry as any other member in the House of Commons. It is only a day or two ago that I heard the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) make the statement that the farmers of this country were the only people who were ever asked to sell their products at less than the cost of production. I did not contradict him at that time, but I should now like to say that I myself, on many occasions, have sold fish below the cost of production. I am greatly interested in the fishermen being protected to the extent that they will be able to make a fair living. At the same time I realize that even with this resolution we shall have many problems to face.
I have listened with interest to the hon. members from Newfoundland who have spoken within the last half hour, and from my experience I should like to assure them that it would be utterly impossible for the fishermen in Newfoundland to find a market for their fish in Canada. They will have to look to the same markets they have had over the years in order to dispose of their catch of fish. We in the maritimes have found it utterly impossible to sell any volume of fish in Canada. I have made the statement on the floor of the House of Commons on several occasions that some particular lines of fish that we produce are sold 100 per cent in the United States. That is the natural market for fresh fish, lobster, and all kinds of shellfish. In the dried-fish industry you have a different market that goes farther south. If the fisherman in Newfoundland expects to sell

dried fish during the year 1950, I am convinced in my own mind that he will be obliged to seek a market in that same country.
There is a problem which arises in connection with price control and which has been discussed to a great extent down on the Atlantic coast. As I have stated, we sell practically all we produce in the United States, in competition with fish that are caught in the state of Maine. When this prices board was set up in 1944, all the papers in the state of Maine and along the New England coast line took it up immediately. The great worry among the fishermen in those states at that time was that we in Canada would be selling fish, the price of which was supported in Canada, in competition with Maine fish. They were bitterly opposed to Canadian fishermen having that advantage.
When the time comes, and if it is found necessary to support these prices, I believe that we may find a good deal of opposition in the state of Maine, in trying to compete with those fishermen there. I believe there is some way by means of which the fishermen may be helped to the extent that they can at least sell all they produce at the cost of production. Prior to the war, those engaged in the fishing industry had had many years of distress circumstances. Anything that might be done by this government to assist the fishermen down in that section would certainly be appreciated. But I know that we shall find that opposition from the fishermen in the New England states. I realize that it may be quite a problem and in the final analysis it might be responsible for a duty being placed on Canadian fish going into the United States. If a duty were placed by the United States on any of the fish that we produce, it would practically kill that particular industry down there. I just want to put one set of figures on the record again to indicate the extent to which we depend on those people for markets.
A few years ago-as a matter of fact, in 1948-I obtained the figures from the lobster company in the town in which I live as to the volume of their business transacted in the United States. In that particular year they did $4 million worth of business in lobsters. Of that total 96-4 per cent of the lobster was sold in the United States. Less than 4 per cent was sold in Canada. We have other industries down there-smaller ones I will admit-where 100 per cent of the production is sold in the United States. Legislation that may in any way interfere with the market we have enjoyed over the years would be very harmful to the fishing industry in that section. I am hopeful that this legislation

may not bring about that condition, but at the same time I realize that we certainly will have a lot of opposition from fishermen in the New England states.

speechtext: I notice from the report of last year of the fisheries support board that research activities were carried on in the Gaspe peninsula and on the north shore of the gulf of St. Lawrence and the Magdalen islands in 1948 to find out the relationship between fishermen's incomes and the factors affecting them. I wonder whether any work of that kind was done in Newfoundland during the past year.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: Yes; similar work has been done in Newfoundland, and is going on all the time.
By whom?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
By officials from the
fisheries research board.
At Ottawa?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: Yes, from the prices support board in Ottawa.
Are any applications to the fisheries support board being considered at the present time in relation to any commodities? If so, where are they?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: There is one.
From what district?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: One application came in for consideration a short while ago. It is from British Columbia and has to do with dogfish oil. Last week the board considered one from Newfoundland. It had to do with the salt fish situation.
No decision has been arrived at yet?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
No.

Fisheries Prices Support Act
Would the same support apply to the fish that is exported as it does to the fish that is consumed or sold in Canada?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: I understand that it the fish is to be subsidized it will not be exported.

I may not have got the answer correctly to the question asked by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. Did the parliamentary assistant make a statement with respect to price support and the setting of a ceiling price on fish? Will the minister make a statement on that now?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: I did not hear the hon. member's question. Will he repeat it?

I understood from my colleague that the parliamentary assistant gave an answer to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni with respect to an application from Newfoundland to the prices support board. I did not hear it.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
The parliamentary assistant said that there was an application before the board for a floor price on cod liver oil. That has been considered, but no decision has been rendered.
There is also under consideration what we might do to help the salt fish situation in the province of Newfoundland. No decision has been reached on that, although a recommendation is going forward.
The minister has had a request, has he?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: Yes, we have had a request. I do not know whether it is an official request, but the problem of the Newfoundland salt fish industry is one that has been carefully watched ever since the exchange situation developed, and we are giving it every assistance we possibly can. I think we would have greater success if there was less said about a surplus. You are creating a situation for yourself that makes it very difficult in Newfoundland when you tell the world that you have a long surplus of fish. I would like to tell them now that you have not got a long surplus, and let these people know who are looking for bargains that they are not going to get them.
May I ask the minister who in the house has been making statements about surpluses in Newfoundland?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Everybody who rises in his place.
You have.
I have not.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: I had not intended to say anything on this matter because the parliamentary assistant was handling it. The hon. member for Selkirk implied that we had paid the money to the wholesalers rather than to the fishermen for the fish that were taken in Winnipeg last year. We obtained the names of the fishermen from the wholesalers who brought them in, and the cheques were sent to the individual fishermen, not to the wholesalers. We paid the cold storage people for the storing of the fish. Necessarily we had to bring them in, and they were on consignment there. We had to pay for the storage, but for the fish themselves the cheques went to the individual fishermen.
With your permission, Mr. Chairman, I want to ask the minister another question. These cheques that went out went to the men that collected the fish, not to the men who took the fish from the lake?
What is the difference?
There is a big difference.
It was a poor buy, anyway.

It was not a poor buy at all. I am serious about this. Hon. members can laugh at me as much as they like; I do not care. I would not rise in my place and tell the hon. gentleman he was wrong if I did not know that I am right. I am positive that I am right, because I have been there and I have seen it myself; the men who actually drew the fish out of the lake did not get paid. The men who collected the fish skinned them, passed them on to the packer who got the cream off it. I have another question.
Six o'clock.
I do not want to be heated about this, but I am going to be asked these questions when I go back to Manitoba.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: I will give the hon. member all the information if he asks me in a proper way.
The minister employed a technical consultant three months under the Fisheries Prices Support Act. What was his job? Who was he?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: That is a question that could be answered when our estimates are before the committee. I should be glad to give the information then. We will give all the information. We shall tell you to whom the cheques were sent and how they were distributed.
Will you take the question as notice?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: Yes.

I asked the minister a question a short time ago but he did not answer me.
I should like to have cleared up the suggestion that some hon. member on this side of the house, meaning either the hon. member for St. John's West or myself, has been talking about the fish held in Newfoundland, and that if we did not talk too much about it there would not be so much there. I want to know if the statement was made either by the hon. member for St. John's West or myself.
Carried.
I think the minister should be allowed to answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: There has been a delegation here in connection with fish and that has been known to everybody. You have all said that you are in a difficult position, although probably that was not said in the house.
We are.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: That is all I was talking about.
